claim: Participants may underweight information incompatible with previous choices, a phenomenon called confirmation bias.
source: Previous research has shown that participants may underweight information incompatible with previous choices, a phenomenon called confirmation bias.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Participants sample more information from a previously chosen alternative.
source: We investigate how choice influences information gathering using a perceptual choice task and find that participants sample more information from a previously chosen alternative.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study described in the abstract.

claim: The higher the confidence in the initial choice, the more biased information sampling becomes.
source: Furthermore, the higher the confidence in the initial choice, the more biased information sampling becomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: When faced with the possibility of revising an earlier decision, participants are more likely to stick with their original choice, even when incorrect.
source: As a consequence, when faced with the possibility of revising an earlier decision, participants are more likely to stick with their original choice, even when incorrect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between sampling bias and subsequent choice.

claim: Agency controls the phenomenon of biased information sampling affecting subsequent choice.
source: Critically, we show that agency controls this phenomenon.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing free sampling and fixed sampling conditions.

claim: The effect of biased sampling on subsequent choice disappears in a fixed sampling condition where presentation of evidence is controlled by the experimenter.
source: The effect disappears in a fixed sampling condition where presentation of evidence is controlled by the experimenter, suggesting that the way in which confirmatory evidence is acquired critically impacts the decision process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 comparing free and fixed sampling conditions.

claim: Active information acquisition plays a critical role in the propagation of strongly held beliefs over time.
source: These results suggest active information acquisition plays a critical role in the propagation of strongly held beliefs over time.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings about agency and sampling bias.

claim: An agent should look for information to maximally reduce their uncertainty.
source: In theory, an agent should look for information to maximally reduce their uncertainty (Schulz and Gershman, 2019; Schwartenbeck et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2016 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work in the field.

claim: There is some evidence that humans look for information to maximally reduce their uncertainty.
source: There is some evidence that this is indeed what humans do (Kobayashi and Hsu, 2019; Meyer and Shi, 1995; Steyvers et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: A range of other drivers of information search have been identified that make us deviate from the sampling behaviour of optimal agents.
source: but a range of other drivers of information search have been identified that make us deviate from the sampling behaviour of optimal agents (Eliaz and Schotter, 2007; Gesiarz et al., 2019; Hunt et al., 2016; Kobayashi et al., 2019; Rodriguez Cabrero et al., 2019; Sharot, 2011; van Lieshout et al., 2018; Wang and Hayden, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Confirmation bias is defined as the tendency of agents to seek out or overweight evidence that aligns with their beliefs while avoiding or underweighting evidence that contradicts them.
source: Confirmation bias is defined as the tendency of agents to seek out or overweight evidence that aligns with their beliefs while avoiding or underweighting evidence that contradicts them (Hart et al., 2009; Lord et al., 1979; Nickerson, 1998; Stroud, 2007; Wason, 1960; Wason, 1968).
evidence: This claim is a definition supported by citations to foundational work on confirmation bias.

claim: Confirmation bias has often been described in the context of what media people choose to consume.
source: This effect has often been described in the context of what media people choose to consume (Bakshy et al., 2015; Bennett and Iyengar, 2008; Pariser, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on media consumption.

claim: Sensitivity to new information has been shown to decrease after choice.
source: For example, sensitivity to new information has been shown to decrease after choice (Bronfman et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Sensitivity to a stimulus is increased when it is consistent with the stimulus presented before.
source: while Talluri et al., 2018 have shown that sensitivity to a stimulus is increased when it is consistent with the stimulus presented before.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Learning rates were found to be higher for feedback indicating positive obtained outcomes as well as for negative forgone outcomes.
source: Furthermore, in Palminteri et al., 2017a learning rates were found to be higher for feedback indicating positive obtained outcomes as well as for negative forgone outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Confirmation bias during learning might be adaptive in some contexts.
source: This effect has been replicated in recent studies that suggest confirmation bias during learning might be adaptive in some contexts (Tarantola et al., 2021; Lefebvre et al., 2020; Salem-Garica et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Most of the existing research on perceptual decision-making has focused on the weighting of incoming information during evidence accumulation or belief updating.
source: Most of the existing research on perceptual decision-making has focused on the weighting of incoming information during evidence accumulation or belief updating.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature in the field.

claim: Agents also actively search for confirmatory evidence.
source: Other findings suggest that agents also actively search for confirmatory evidence (Hunt et al., 2016; Hunt et al., 2018; Tolcott et al., 1989; Wason, 1968)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on active information search.

claim: None of the experiments investigating active search for confirmatory evidence investigated the effect of biased information sampling in simple, perceptual choice.
source: but none of these experiments investigated the effect of biased information sampling in simple, perceptual choice.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature and identifies a gap.

claim: It is unclear whether confirmation bias arises from evidence underweighting, biased information sampling, or both.
source: As most paradigms currently used to study confirmation bias do not explicitly focus on active information sampling performed by the agent, therefore it is unclear whether confirmation bias arises from evidence underweighting, biased information sampling, or both.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the limitations of existing research paradigms.

claim: Confidence is known to play an important role in guiding decisions.
source: Confidence is known to play an important role in guiding decisions (Bogacz et al., 2010; Boldt et al., 2019; Folke et al., 2016; Rabbitt, 1966; Yeung and Summerfield, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on confidence in decision-making.

claim: Confidence may guide the information search preceding choice.
source: It is therefore likely it may also guide the information search preceding choice (Desender et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the role of confidence in decision-making, supported by a citation.

claim: Confidence affects a neural signal of confirmatory evidence integration.
source: In fact, Rollwage et al., 2020 recently showed that confidence indeed affects a neural signal of confirmatory evidence integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The higher confidence is in a choice, the stronger the decision-maker's belief is in the correctness of this choice.
source: By definition, the higher confidence is in a choice, the stronger the decision-maker's belief is in the correctness of this choice (Fleming and Lau, 2014; Pouget et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: Confirmation bias in information sampling will be stronger after choices made with high confidence.
source: Accordingly, we predict that confirmation bias in information sampling will be stronger after choices made with high confidence.
evidence: This is a prediction based on inference from the definition of confidence.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants' performance was highly sensitive to the amount of perceptual evidence presented in a given trial.
source: As expected, participants' performance was highly sensitive to the amount of perceptual evidence presented in a given trial (i.e. the difference in the amount of dots in the left and right patches; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants were more accurate in the second choice compared to the first choice.
source: Participants were also more accurate in the second choice compared to the first choice, showing that they used the additional sampling time between choice phases to accumulate additional perceptual evidence that allowed them to increase accuracy on the second choice (t27 = 8.74, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants used the additional sampling time between choice phases to accumulate additional perceptual evidence that allowed them to increase accuracy on the second choice.
source: Participants were also more accurate in the second choice compared to the first choice, showing that they used the additional sampling time between choice phases to accumulate additional perceptual evidence that allowed them to increase accuracy on the second choice (t27 = 8.74, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observed increase in accuracy.

claim: In Experiment 1, during the sampling phase, participants spent more time viewing the patch they chose in the first decision phase relative to the unchosen alternative.
source: In line with this hypothesis, during the sampling phase, participants spent more time viewing the patch they chose in the first decision phase relative to the unchosen alternative (Figure 1C; t27 = 7.28, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant interaction between choice and confidence, such that the higher the degree of confidence was in the first choice, the more sampling was biased in favour of that choice.
source: In a hierarchical regression predicting sampling time difference between the chosen and unchosen stimulus, we found a significant interaction between choice and confidence, such that the higher the degree of confidence was in the first choice, the more sampling was biased in favour of that choice (Figure 2; t26.96=5.26, p < 0.001; see Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In Experiment 1, sampling time difference affected confidence in the second choice, such that the stronger sampling bias was towards the initially chosen stimulus, the higher confidence in the second choice if that same stimulus was chosen again.
source: Besides this, sampling time difference in turn affected confidence in the second choice, such that the stronger sampling bias was towards the initially chosen stimulus, the higher confidence in the second choice if that same stimulus was chosen again (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; t26.01=9.40, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: In Experiment 1, change of mind was a significant negative predictor of the second confidence rating.
source: Change of mind was a significant negative predictor of the second confidence rating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; t23.66=-10.41, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a negative interaction effect between sampling time difference and change of mind on the second confidence rating.
source: Also, a negative interaction effect between sampling time difference and change of mind on the second confidence rating was observed, meaning that the effect of sampling bias on confidence was reversed in trials where participants changed their mind (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; t24.48=-10.21, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant main positive effect of choice on sampling time difference, such that a chosen stimulus was likely to be sampled for longer during the sampling phase.
source: We also saw a significant main positive effect of choice on sampling time difference, such that a chosen stimulus was likely to be sampled for longer during the sampling phase (Figure 2B; t26.96=9.64, p < 0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant main positive effect of evidence difference on sampling time difference, whereby the correct stimulus (containing the most dots) was sampled for longer.
source: There was also a significant main positive effect of evidence difference on sampling time difference, whereby the correct stimulus (containing the most dots) was sampled for longer (Figure 2B; t26.96=13.02, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Experiment 1, bias in sampling time towards the previously chosen option was predictive of future choice.
source: Using a multinomial hierarchical logistic regression, we found that bias in sampling time towards the previously chosen option was indeed predictive of future choice. In other words, the more participants sampled a previously chosen option, the more likely they were to choose it again (Figure 2C; z = −11.0, p < 0.001; see Appendix 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Experiment 1, evidence difference and confidence were significantly negatively related to subsequent changes of mind.
source: Furthermore, evidence difference and confidence were significantly negatively related to subsequent changes of mind, whereby participants were less likely to change their mind if their initial choice was correct and if it was made with high confidence (Figure 2C; main effect of evidence difference – z = −3.06, p < 0.01, main effect of confidence – z = −10.12, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants were sensitive to the difficulty of the given trials.
source: Again, participants were sensitive to the difficulty of the given trials (Figure 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants were more accurate on the second choice compared to the first choice.
source: and were more accurate on the second choice compared to the first choice (t17 = 6.80, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, in the free sampling condition, participants spent more time viewing the patch they just chose.
source: We also replicated our main result in the free sampling condition showing that participants spent more time viewing the patch they just chose (Figure 3C; t17 = 3.52, p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In Experiment 2, the size of sampling time bias was proportional to the total amount of sampling time available.
source: Furthermore, the size of this sampling time bias was proportional to the total amount of sampling time available in study 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no particular period of time within the sampling phase where confirmatory information sampling was more likely.
source: suggesting that there was no particular period of time within the sampling phase where confirmatory information sampling was more likely contrary to our expectation.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observation that sampling bias was proportional to total sampling time.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a significant interaction between choice and confidence in the free sampling condition.
source: This new experiment also replicated the mediating effect of confidence on how sampling bias affects subsequent choice. We again found a significant interaction between choice and confidence (Figure 4A–B; t16.97 = 4.29, p < 0.001; see supplemental materials Appendix 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In Experiment 2, there were main positive effects of choice and evidence difference on sampling time difference between the chosen and unchosen stimulus.
source: and replicated the main positive effects of choice and evidence difference on sampling time difference between the chosen and unchosen stimulus (Figure 4B; main effect of choice: t16.97 = 2.90, p < 0.01; main effect of evidence difference: t16.97= 9.21, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Experiment 2, confidence negatively predicted the total amount of time spent sampling.
source: Confidence was also shown to negatively predict the total amount of time spent sampling, that is, the total time actually spent gazing at the two stimuli during the sampling phase (rather than the central fixation cross; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; t22.99 = –4.01, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: In Experiment 2, change of mind negatively predicted confidence in the second choice phase.
source: Change of mind also negatively predicted confidence in the second choice phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; t16.17 = –6.16, p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a positive effect of sampling time difference on the second confidence rating.
source: and there was again a positive effect of sampling time difference on the second confidence rating (t17.03 = 5.79, p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a significant negative interaction effect between change of mind and sampling time difference on the second confidence rating.
source: as well as a significant negative interaction effect between change of mind and sampling time difference (t24.55 = –3.96, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a negative effect of sampling bias on subsequent change of mind in the free sampling condition.
source: Similarly, we replicated the negative effect of sampling bias on subsequent change of mind (Figure 4C; z = −7.20, p < 0.001; see Appendix 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In Experiment 2, there were main negative effects of evidence difference and confidence on change of mind.
source: as well as the main negative effects of evidence difference and confidence on change of mind (Figure 4C; main effect of evidence difference: z = −2.66, p < 0.01; main effect of confidence: z = −8.73, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The uncertainty around an internal estimate scales with numerosity.
source: It has been shown that the uncertainty around an internal estimate scales with numerosity (Scott et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: In Experiment 1, total numerosity did not have a significant effect on sampling bias.
source: We found that neither total numerosity (experiment 1: t12.71=-1.77, p = 0.10; experiment 2: t25.07=0.62, p = 0.54)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, total numerosity did not have a significant effect on sampling bias.
source: We found that neither total numerosity (experiment 1: t12.71=-1.77, p = 0.10; experiment 2: t25.07=0.62, p = 0.54)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1, the number of dots of the chosen option did not have a significant effect on sampling bias.
source: or the number of dots of the chosen option (experiment 1: t71.10=-1.82, p = 0.07; experiment 2: t87.40=0.25, p = 0.81) had a significant effect on sampling bias
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the number of dots of the chosen option did not have a significant effect on sampling bias.
source: or the number of dots of the chosen option (experiment 1: t71.10=-1.82, p = 0.07; experiment 2: t87.40=0.25, p = 0.81) had a significant effect on sampling bias
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Participants' sampling was not biased by a drive to reduce uncertainty by sampling the option with more dots.
source: meaning that participants' sampling was not biased by a drive to reduce uncertainty by sampling the option with more dots.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the lack of effect of numerosity on sampling bias.

claim: In a previous study, there was a significant effect of choice on sampling time difference in both the 'most' frame and the 'fewest' frame.
source: In this dataset, we found a significant effect of choice on sampling time difference in both frames ('most' frame: t57.54=24.01, p < 0.001; 'fewest' frame: t33.72=14.97, p < 0.001; Figure 4—figure supplement 8)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from a previous study.

claim: In a previous study, there was no significant effect of the total number of dots on sampling time difference in either the 'most' frame or the 'fewest' frame.
source: and no significant effect of the total number of dots on sampling time difference ('most' frame: t31.41=-0.37, p = 0.72; 'fewest' frame: t40.01=1.49, p = 0.14)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from a previous study.

claim: Numerosity is not significantly affecting the sampling process in this task.
source: Overall, these results seem to indicate that numerosity is not significantly affecting the sampling process in this task.
evidence: This claim is an inference from multiple analyses showing no effect of numerosity.

claim: In Experiment 2, presentation order in the initial sampling phase did not affect sampling time difference.
source: To exclude this possibility, we performed a regression analysis predicting sampling time difference as a function of presentation order in experiment 2 and found no effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 9; t49.65=0.08, p = 0.93).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, in the fixed-viewing condition, the amount of time spent viewing the patches in the sampling phase did not significantly affect subsequent choice.
source: In line with the second prediction, we found that in the fixed-viewing condition, contrary to the free-sampling condition in this experiment and in the first experiment, the amount of time spent viewing the patches in the sampling phase did not significantly affect subsequent choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the main effect of sampling bias on change of mind was completely offset by the positive effect of the interaction term between sampling bias and the fixed-viewing condition dummy variable.
source: In a multinomial hierarchical logistic regression predicting change of mind from the first choice phase to the second choice phase within a given trial, the main effect of sampling bias on change of mind was completely offset by the positive effect of the interaction term between sampling bias and a dummy variable that was set to 1 if a trial was in the fixed-viewing condition (Figure 4C–D; z = 6.77, p < 0.001; see Appendix 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no effect of sampling bias on change of mind in the fixed-viewing condition.
source: This means that there was no effect of sampling bias on change of mind in the fixed-viewing condition.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the statistical analysis showing the interaction effect.

claim: In Experiment 2, the number of saccades made within each patch during the sampling phase was higher in the fixed-viewing condition than in the main experiment.
source: We found that the number of saccades was actually higher in the fixed-viewing condition than in the main experiment (t17 = −4.22, p < 0.001), which means participants were indeed exploring the information in this condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: In Experiment 2, no significant difference in accuracy was observed between the free sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: Furthermore, no significant difference in accuracy was observed between the two conditions (t17 = 1.51, p = 0.14)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, sensitivity to decision evidence was slightly higher in the second choice in the free sampling condition compared to the fixed sampling condition.
source: though sensitivity to decision evidence was slightly higher in the second choice in the free sampling condition compared to the fixed sampling condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the number of changes of mind was equal between the free sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: The number of changes of mind was also equal between the two conditions (t17 = 0.75, p = 0.47)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, confidence ratings in the first choice were not significantly different between the free sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: as well as both confidence ratings (confidence in first choice: t17 = −1.38, p = 0.19; confidence in second choice: t17 = 0.5, p = 0.62; for more details see Figure 4—figure supplements 10–12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, confidence ratings in the second choice were not significantly different between the free sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: as well as both confidence ratings (confidence in first choice: t17 = −1.38, p = 0.19; confidence in second choice: t17 = 0.5, p = 0.62; for more details see Figure 4—figure supplements 10–12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The GLAM model correctly captured the reaction times and choice behaviour of the participants at group-level both in the free-sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: The model correctly captured the reaction times (RT) and choice behaviour of the participants at group-level both in the free-sampling (Figure 5B) and fixed-viewing conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The GLAM model predicted faster RTs when trial difficulty was low in both free-sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: More specifically, we found that the model predicted faster RTs when trial difficulty was low (|ΔDots| is high; Figure 5B–C, top left).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The GLAM model reproduced overall choice behaviour as a function of the number of dots in the patches in both free-sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: The model also reproduced overall choice behaviour as a function of the number of dots in the patches (ΔDots = DotsLeft – DotsRight) in both conditions (Figure 5B–C, top right).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Gaze allocation predicted the probability of choosing the correct patch in the free-sampling condition.
source: Furthermore, we found gaze allocation (ΔGaze = gLeft – gRight) predicted the probability of choosing the correct patch in the free-sampling condition (Figure 5C, bottom left).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Gaze influence estimated from participant's behaviour was higher in the free-sampling than in the fixed-viewing condition.
source: We found GI estimated purely from participant's behaviour was higher in the free-sampling than in the fixed-viewing condition (comparing average GI by participant, free-sampling condition: Mean = 0.148, SD = 0.169; fixed-viewing condition: Mean = 0.016, SD = 0.14; t17 = 2.708, p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The effect of visual attention on choice was higher in the free-sampling condition.
source: This suggests the effect of visual attention on choice was higher in the free-sampling condition.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the higher gaze influence in the free-sampling condition.

claim: The GLAM model predicted a higher gaze influence on corrected choice probability in the free-sampling condition compared to the fixed-viewing condition.
source: In line with this, the model also predicted a higher GI on corrected choice probability in the free-sampling condition (comparing average GI by individual model predictions, free-sampling condition: Mean = 0.112, SD = 0.106; fixed-viewing condition: Mean = 0.033, SD = 0.028; t17 = 2.853, p < 0.05; Figure 5B–C, bottom right).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: There was a significant variation in the gaze bias parameter between the free-sampling and fixed-viewing conditions, indicating a higher influence of gaze on choice in the free-sampling condition.
source: We found a significant variation in the gaze bias parameter (Mean γ Free = 0.81, Mean γ Fixed = 0.98, t17 = –3.934; p < 0.01), indicating a higher influence of gaze on choice in the free-sampling condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters.

claim: During the fixed-viewing condition, the parameter γ ≈ 1 indicates that almost no gaze bias was present on those trials.
source: Note that during the fixed-viewing condition, the parameter γ ≈ 1 indicates that almost no gaze bias was present on those trials.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the model parameter value.

claim: There was no significant difference in the evidence scaling parameter (τ) between the free-sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: Conversely, there was no significant difference for the other parameters between the conditions (Mean τFree = 1.44, τFixed=1.13, t17 = 1.003; p = 0.32, n.s.;
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters.

claim: There was no significant difference in the noise standard deviation parameter (σ) between the free-sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
source: Mean σFree = 0.0077, Mean σFixed=0.0076, t17 = 0.140; p = 0.89, n.s.;
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters.

claim: There was no significant difference in the drift term parameter (ν) between the free-sampling and fixed-viewing conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters.

claim: Gathering information actively does not affect the overall speed at which information is integrated, but it specifically modulates the likelihood of choosing the gazed-at option.
source: These results suggest that gathering information actively (i.e. free-sampling condition) does not affect the overall speed at which information is integrated, but it specifically modulates the likelihood of choosing the gazed-at option.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the model parameter comparisons.

claim: The identified effect of gaze bias did not depend on a less variable gaze time range.
source: Finally, to test that the identified effect did not depend on a less variable gaze time range we resampled the data from the free-sampling condition to match the gaze time range in the fixed-viewing condition, and fitted the GLAM again. We replicated our finding even when the gaze time range in the free-sampling condition was reduced to match that in the fixed-viewing condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional model fitting analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: A form of confirmation bias exists in active information sampling, and not just in information weighting.
source: In this work, we have demonstrated that a form of confirmation bias exists in active information sampling, and not just in information weighting as previously shown.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main finding supported by the experimental data.

claim: The sampling bias effect is robust for simple perceptual choice.
source: Using two novel experiments we showed that this effect is robust for simple perceptual choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from two independent experiments.

claim: The sampling bias affects future choice.
source: Critically we show that this sampling bias affects future choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between sampling bias and subsequent choice.

claim: The effect of sampling bias on subsequent choice is only present in the free-sampling condition.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that this effect is only present in the free-sampling condition, showing that agency is essential for biased sampling to have an effect on subsequent choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing free and fixed sampling conditions.

claim: Agency is essential for biased sampling to have an effect on subsequent choice.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that this effect is only present in the free-sampling condition, showing that agency is essential for biased sampling to have an effect on subsequent choice.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the difference between free and fixed sampling conditions.

claim: Preference for confirmatory evidence has previously mostly been studied in the context of strongly held political, religious or lifestyle beliefs, and not in perceptual decision-making.
source: Preference for confirmatory evidence has previously mostly been studied in the context of strongly held political, religious or lifestyle beliefs, and not in perceptual decision-making (Bakshy et al., 2015; Hart et al., 2009; Lord et al., 1979; Nickerson, 1998; Stroud, 2007; Wason, 1960, Wason, 1968).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature supported by citations.

claim: Confirmation bias in information search is present even in decisions where the beliefs formed by participants are not meaningful to their daily lives.
source: Our results, together with the recent work of others (Talluri et al., 2018; Palminteri et al., 2017b; Lefebvre et al., 2020), show that confirmation bias in information search is present even in decisions where the beliefs formed by participants are not meaningful to their daily lives.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current experimental data and citations to related work.

claim: Confirmation bias might be a fundamental property of information sampling, existing irrespective of how important the belief is to the agent.
source: This suggests that confirmation bias might be a fundamental property of information sampling, existing irrespective of how important the belief is to the agent.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observation that confirmation bias occurs even in simple perceptual tasks.

claim: Biases in information sampling might arise from Pavlovian approach, a behavioural strategy that favours approaching choice alternatives associated with reward.
source: Recent findings suggest that biases in information sampling might arise from Pavlovian approach, a behavioural strategy that favours approaching choice alternatives associated with reward (Hunt et al., 2016; Rutledge et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on citations to related work.

claim: The number of hypotheses an individual can consider in parallel is likely to be limited.
source: Furthermore, the number of hypotheses an individual can consider in parallel is likely to be limited (Tweney et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to previous work.

claim: It may be advantageous to first attempt to rule out the dominant hypothesis before going on to sample from alternative options.
source: As such, it may be advantageous to first attempt to rule out the dominant hypothesis before going on to sample from alternative options.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the potential adaptive value of the observed behavior.

claim: The sampling bias could be the solution to an exploit-explore dilemma in which the decision-maker must decide when to stop 'exploiting' a particular hypothesis and instead 'explore' different ones.
source: In this vein, the sampling bias we see could be the solution to an exploit-explore dilemma in which the decision-maker must decide when to stop 'exploiting' a particular hypothesis (on which stimulus has the most dots) and instead 'explore' different ones.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the potential explanation for the observed behavior.

claim: Active information sampling plays a key role in the amplification of beliefs from one decision to the next.
source: Our findings show that active information sampling plays a key role in the amplification of beliefs from one decision to the next, and that changes in evidence weighting likely only account for part of observed confirmation bias effects.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Changes in evidence weighting likely only account for part of observed confirmation bias effects.
source: Our findings show that active information sampling plays a key role in the amplification of beliefs from one decision to the next, and that changes in evidence weighting likely only account for part of observed confirmation bias effects.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Confidence modulated the confirmation bias effect, such that choices made with higher confidence, led to increased sampling of the chosen option and an increased likelihood of choosing the same option again in the second choice phase.
source: We show that confidence modulated the confirmation bias effect, such that choices made with higher confidence, led to increased sampling of the chosen option and an increased likelihood of choosing the same option again in the second choice phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both experiments.

claim: The strength with which a belief is held determines the size of the confirmation bias in active information sampling.
source: This shows that the strength with which a belief is held determines the size of the confirmation bias in active information sampling.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the relationship between confidence and sampling bias.

claim: Confidence affects the integration of confirmatory evidence as reflected in MEG recordings of brain activity during evidence accumulation.
source: Confidence has previously been shown to affect the integration of confirmatory evidence as reflected in MEG recordings of brain activity during evidence accumulation (Rollwage et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Recent work in economics and neuroscience have given theoretical and experimental proof of a relationship between overconfidence, and extreme political beliefs.
source: Furthermore, recent work in economics and neuroscience have given theoretical and experimental proof of a relationship between overconfidence, and extreme political beliefs (Ortoleva and Snowberg, 2015; Rollwage et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in economics and neuroscience.

claim: Altered information sampling could be the missing link between overconfidence and extreme political beliefs.
source: Our results suggest altered information sampling could be the missing link between these two phenomena.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on inference from the current findings and previous work.

claim: Overconfidence in a belief would lead to increased sampling of confirmatory evidence in line with that belief, which in turn would lead to even higher confidence.
source: Specifically, given that we have shown that increased confidence leads to increased confirmation bias, it follows that overconfidence in a belief would lead to increased sampling of confirmatory evidence in line with that belief, which in turn would lead to even higher confidence.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observed relationship between confidence and sampling bias.

claim: It is not sufficient that agents freely make a choice for that choice to bias future decisions.
source: We also show that it is not sufficient that agents freely make a choice for that choice to bias future decisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the fixed sampling condition.

claim: Integration of evidence into beliefs is dependent on whether the agent has actively chosen to sample this information.
source: This suggests that integration of evidence into beliefs is dependent on whether the agent has actively chosen to sample this information.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the difference between free and fixed sampling conditions.

claim: A sense of agency appears to impact the extent to which new information influences future choice.
source: In other words, a sense of agency appears to impact the extent to which new information influences future choice (Hassall et al., 2019; Chambon et al., 2020; Doll et al., 2011; Cockburn et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is an inference from the current findings supported by citations to related work.

claim: Making a choice may not necessarily lead to confirmation bias if it is not followed by active decisions to sample evidence in line with that choice.
source: and making a choice may not necessarily lead to confirmation bias if it is not followed by active decisions to sample evidence in line with that choice.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: In a previous study by Chambon et al., 2020, confirmation bias in learning rates was only present when participants were able to freely choose between stimuli and not when these choices were fixed by the experimenter.
source: Our results are in line with Chambon et al., 2020, in which confirmation bias in learning rates was only present when participants were able to freely choose between stimuli and not when these choices were fixed by the experimenter.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Choice commitment affects subsequent decisions to sample.
source: Our results expand on these findings, by showing that choice commitment also affects subsequent decisions to sample, and that the resulting biased sampling influences future choices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current experimental data.

claim: Biased sampling influences future choices.
source: Our results expand on these findings, by showing that choice commitment also affects subsequent decisions to sample, and that the resulting biased sampling influences future choices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current experimental data.

claim: Active information sampling is likely to play a central role in the propagation of confirmation bias across decisions.
source: This means that active information sampling is likely to play a central role in the propagation of confirmation bias across decisions, as seen in our descriptive economic model (see Appendix 3).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings and the descriptive model.

claim: It is less clear to what extent the ability to freely sample and any resulting confirmation bias might be beneficial or detrimental to choice accuracy.
source: It is less clear, however, to what extent the ability to freely sample and any resulting confirmation bias might be beneficial or detrimental to choice accuracy, as in our task there was no clear difference in accuracy between the free and fixed sampling conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that accuracy did not differ between conditions.

claim: A specific boost in the accumulation of evidence of the visually attended items was found in the free sampling condition.
source: Additionally, the results from the GLAM model show that, in line with previous studies (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich et al., 2010; Sepulveda et al., 2020; Tavares et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2019), a specific boost in the accumulation of evidence of the visually attended items was found in the free sampling condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting results and citations to previous studies.

claim: A disconnection between an item's sampling time and evidence accumulation was found in the fixed condition.
source: Conversely, a disconnection between an item's sampling time and evidence accumulation was found in the fixed condition (i.e. the absence of gaze bias in GLAM implies that visual fixations did not affect evidence integration when the sampling was not controlled by the decision-maker).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting results.

claim: Attentional allocation itself is directed towards the options that the participants reckon more relevant for the task to be performed.
source: One explanation for this result is that attentional allocation itself is directed towards the options that the participants reckon more relevant for the task to be performed (Sepulveda et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: Participants perceived the goal of the second choice to be slightly different from the goal of the first: in the second case they had to verify whether their initial choice was correct, as well as finding the patch with the most dots.
source: In our experiment, the goal of the task was theoretically identical for the first and second choice (i.e. to find the patch with more dots). However, in agreement with the ideas of our descriptive economic model, it could be that participants perceived the goal of the second choice to be slightly different from the goal of the first: in the second case they had to verify whether their initial choice was correct, as well as finding the patch with the most dots.
evidence: This claim is speculation about participants' perception of the task.

claim: In the fixed sampling condition, the difference in display time of the items is ignored or cannot be consistently integrated in the decision process because participant's attention allocation is not necessarily associated with their goals.
source: On the other hand, since in the fixed sampling condition participant's attention allocation is not necessarily associated with their goals, the difference in display time of the items is ignored or cannot be consistently integrated in their decision process.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the mechanism in the fixed sampling condition.

claim: Recent models characterize attention's role as lowering the variance of the accumulated evidence towards the attended option, which in turn updates the internal belief.
source: A complementary perspective has been given in recent work by Jang et al., 2021 and Callaway et al., 2021. Their models characterize attention's role as lowering the variance of the accumulated evidence towards the attended option, which in turn updates the internal belief.
evidence: This claim is based on citations to recent modeling work.

claim: Recent models characterize attention as an internally generated factor that is allocated following optimal sampling policies.
source: Crucially, they have characterized attention as an internally generated factor that is allocated following optimal sampling policies, unlike other models that take attention as an exogenous factor (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich et al., 2010; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to recent modeling work and contrasts with earlier models.

claim: The exogenous sampling pattern imposed in the experiment might not be aligned with the optimal evolution of the internal beliefs of participants, therefore, the 'offered' evidence is misaligned and therefore does not impact choice.
source: Perhaps, in a similar way to the proposition above in relation to internal goals, it could be the case that the exogenous sampling pattern we imposed in our experiment is not aligned with the optimal evolution of the internal beliefs of participants, therefore, the 'offered' evidence is misaligned and therefore does not impact choice.
evidence: This claim is speculation about why the fixed sampling condition did not show the same effect.

claim: Gaze allocation itself might be used as additional evidence in favour of a choice alternative in a way similar to previous choice.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that gaze allocation itself is used as additional evidence in favour of a choice alternative in a way similar to previous choice as in our descriptive model (see Appendix 3).
evidence: This claim is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: When an agent has previously attended to a choice alternative, this is used as evidence in favour of that option in and of itself.
source: This would mean that when an agent has previously attended to a choice alternative, this is used as evidence in favour of that option in and of itself.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: When gaze allocation is not under the agent's control, as in the fixed-viewing condition, it is not used to inform choice.
source: Therefore, when gaze allocation is not under the agent's control, as in the fixed-viewing condition, it is not used to inform choice.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the mechanism in the fixed-viewing condition.

claim: Agency plays a clear role in evidence accumulation, and consequently in confirmation bias.
source: Our findings imply that agency plays a clear role in evidence accumulation, and consequently in confirmation bias.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Common experimental designs in which information is provided by the experimenter and passively sampled by the participant might not be an ecological way to study decision-making.
source: It also suggests that common experimental designs in which information is provided by the experimenter and passively sampled by the participant might not be an ecological way to study decision-making.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the findings about the importance of agency.

claim: Common experimental designs mask the potentially large effect of active information search on belief formation and choice.
source: These tasks mask the potentially large effect of active information search on belief formation and choice.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the findings about the importance of agency.

claim: People were less likely to share false information online if they had been asked to rate the accuracy of a headline just previously.
source: Pennycook et al., 2021 recently showed that people were less likely to share false information online if they had been asked to rate the accuracy of a headline just previously.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: It may be possible to reduce confirmation bias in information search by priming participants to attend more to accuracy instead of confirmatory evidence.
source: It may therefore be possible to reduce confirmation bias in information search in a similar way by priming participants to attend more to accuracy instead of confirmatory evidence.
evidence: This claim is speculation about potential interventions based on related work.

claim: Participants sampled more information from chosen options in a perceptual choice paradigm.
source: To summarise our findings, we observed that participants sampled more information from chosen options in a perceptual choice paradigm
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Sampling bias predicted subsequent choice.
source: and that this sampling bias predicted subsequent choice.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Asymmetric sampling in favour of the chosen alternative was stronger the higher participants' confidence in this choice.
source: Asymmetric sampling in favour of the chosen alternative was stronger the higher participants' confidence in this choice.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The effect of information on subsequent choice was only seen in a version of the task where participants could sample freely.
source: Furthermore, the effect of information on subsequent choice was only seen in a version of the task where participants could sample freely
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Agency plays an important role in the propagation of strongly held beliefs over time.
source: suggesting agency plays an important role in the propagation of strongly held beliefs over time.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Confirmatory information processing might stem from a general information sampling strategy used to seek information to strengthen prior beliefs rather than from altered weighting during evidence accumulation only.
source: These findings suggest that confirmatory information processing might stem from a general information sampling strategy used to seek information to strengthen prior beliefs rather than from altered weighting during evidence accumulation only
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Active sampling is essential to the effect of confirmation bias on subsequent choice.
source: and that active sampling is essential to this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing free and fixed sampling conditions.

claim: Biased sampling may cause a continuous cycle of belief reinforcement that can be hard to break.
source: Biased sampling may cause a continuous cycle of belief reinforcement that can be hard to break.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on inference from the findings.

claim: Improving our understanding of biased sampling can help us better explain the roots of extreme political, religious and scientific beliefs in our society.
source: Improving our understanding of this phenomenon can help us better explain the roots of extreme political, religious and scientific beliefs in our society.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: In Experiment 1, thirty participants took part in the study.
source: Thirty participants took part in this study.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1, two participants were excluded from the analysis because they gave the highest possible confidence rating on more than 75% of trials.
source: We excluded two participants from the analysis, because they gave the highest possible confidence rating on more than 75% of trials.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: In Experiment 2, twenty-three participants completed the experiment.
source: Twenty-three participants completed this experiment
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, two participants were excluded from the analysis because they gave the highest possible confidence rating on more than 75% of trials.
source: of which two were excluded from the analysis, because they gave the highest possible confidence rating on more than 75% of trials.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: In Experiment 2, three participants were excluded because their confidence was a poor predictor of their accuracy in the task.
source: Another three participants were excluded because their confidence was a poor predictor of their accuracy in the task (lower than two standard deviations under the mean coefficient predicting accuracy in a logistic regression).
evidence: This is a factual statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: In Experiment 1, the computer task consisted of 200 trials.
source: The computer task used in this study consisted of 200 trials.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1, stimuli were presented once for 700ms each in the first presentation phase.
source: Stimuli were presented once for 700ms each in the first presentation phase, with the order of presentation assigned randomly.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants could freely sample the stimuli for 4000ms in the second phase.
source: This was followed by the second phase in which participants could sample the stimuli freely for 4000ms by using the arrow keys to alternately view the stimuli.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1, the dot difference between the two patches was calibrated such that accuracy level within each participant was maintained at 70% throughout the task using a one-up two-down staircase procedure.
source: We calibrated the dot difference between the two patches such that accuracy level within each participant was maintained at 70% throughout the task using a one-up two-down staircase procedure (Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, in the initial presentation phase each stimulus was presented for 500ms.
source: In this version, in the initial presentation phase each stimulus was presented for 500ms.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, the sampling phase between the two choices randomly varied and was either 3000, 5000, or 7000ms.
source: The sampling phase between the two choices randomly varied in this task, and was either 3000, 5000, or 7000ms.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, in one-third of trials in the control condition, the patches were shown an equal amount of time; in two-thirds of trials, one patch was shown three times longer than the other.
source: In one-third of trials, the patches were shown an equal amount of time; in two-thirds of trials, one patch was shown three times longer than the other.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants took part in two sessions, each consisting of 189 trials.
source: Participants took part in two sessions, each consisting of 189 trials.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, eye movements were recorded at a rate of 1000 Hz using an EyeLink 1000 Plus eye-tracker.
source: In experiment 2, we recorded eye movements at a rate of 1000 Hz using an EyeLink 1000 Plus eye-tracker.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Trials with the shortest sampling phase length of 3000ms in experiment 2 were excluded from all analyses, because this time was too short for participants to be able to saccade to each circle more than once.
source: Trials with the shortest sampling phase length of 3000ms in experiment 2 were excluded from all analyses, because it became apparent that this time was too short for participants to be able to saccade to each circle more than once.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: The GLAM model belongs to the family of race models with an additional modulation by visual attention.
source: GLAM belongs to the family of race models with an additional modulation by visual attention (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the model used.

claim: GLAM is an approximation of the attentional Drift Diffusion Model (aDDM).
source: It is an approximation of a widely used class of models – the attentional Drift Diffusion Model (aDDM; Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011)
evidence: This is a factual statement about the model used, supported by citations.

claim: In GLAM, the full dynamic sequence of fixations is replaced by the percentage of time spent fixating the choice alternatives.
source: in which the full dynamic sequence of fixations is replaced by the percentage of time spent fixating the choice alternatives.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the model used.

claim: Even-numbered trials were used to fit the GLAM model while odd-numbered trials were used to test it.
source: Even-numbered trials were used to fit the model while odd-numbered trials were used to test it.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the modeling procedure.
